quarterly_data.signal: CRESCENT ISLAND DELIBERATELY SKIPS HBM AND GDDR FOR LOW-POWER DDR: Anil Nanduri, VP of AI Products and Go-To-Market for Intel's Data Center, described Intel's inference GPU roadmap scaling up from the Arc series to Crescent Island and said that 'with Crescent Island, we intentionally chose low-power DDR instead of GDDR or HBM memory' to land on an energy- and cost-efficient point rather than ultra-premium low-latency tokens - a PCIe card an enterprise can plug in and scale. He positioned the portfolio as Xeon plus Crescent Island plus the SambaNova partnership (SambaNova serving the high-interactivity, high-volume token pipe), sold on TCO and ROI rather than peak performance, deployable from on-prem to a neocloud.
quarterly_data.figure: low-power DDR instead of GDDR or HBM memory

quarterly_data.signal: INTEL'S EXPLANATION OF THE CPU SHORTAGE - AGENTIC WORKLOADS RUN ON CPUs BETWEEN TOKEN GENERATIONS: Nanduri said that in agentic systems the tokens produce outcomes that must be executed and verified, and 'CPUs start to play a lot of role because CPUs are their execution engine, verification engine, and your sandboxing engine. If you see recently why are CPUs in a shortage is because a lot of these back and forth ping pong is happening in the system.' He framed the data-center buildout as four planes - a control plane (orchestrator / agent router / model router / security harness) that runs on CPUs, an agent or data plane for token generation across CPUs, GPUs and RDUs, a network plane where scale-up and scale-out determine wall-clock time as models cross chip boundaries, and a storage plane for databases, KV cache and context memory pooling, all hosted with a CPU - and said memory cost increases have made this balance, rather than raw token throughput, the ROI question for enterprises.
